pos: n. (a name borne by a king of Israel and a king of Judah, both of the house of Ahab — a name that means the LORD hath held, worn by two men who held to Baal)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Achazyah, from 'achaz, to seize or hold fast, and Yah, the covenant name — “the LORD hath grasped” or “whom Jehovah upholds”. Both bearers make the name an irony.
biblical_def: Two kings bear the name Ahaziah, and both belong to the poison that Jezebel introduced into both kingdoms. The first is the son of Ahab and Jezebel, king of Israel for two years, of whom the record says he “walked in the way of his father, and in the way of his mother, and in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat” (1Ki 22:52) — three ways, all downward. His whole reign is compressed into one incident: he fell through a lattice in his upper chamber and, being sick, “sent messengers, and said unto them, Go, enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron whether I shall recover of this disease” (2Ki 1:2). Elijah met the messengers on the road with the question that answers itself: is it because there is no God in Israel? The second is his nephew and namesake, king of Judah, son of Jehoram and of Athaliah the daughter of Ahab, and the verdict is the same house: “he walked in the way of the house of Ahab” (2Ki 8:27). He was visiting Joram in Jezreel when Jehu came, and died of Jehu's arrows at Megiddo (2Ki 9:27). His death put his mother Athaliah on the throne of David, and the line of promise survived in one hidden infant. Two men named “the LORD holds”, and what held them both was Ahab's house.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Ahaziah; in sacred history the name belongs to the eighth king of Israel, son of Ahab, and to the sixth king of Judah, son of Jehoram and Athaliah.
webster_full: AHAZIAH, n. Son of Ahab and Jezebel, and king of Israel two years; the name signifies whom Jehovah upholds.
Falling through a lattice, he sent to enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron, and died as Elijah had said.
Also, the son of Jehoram by Athaliah the daughter of Ahab, and king of Judah one year.
He joined with Joram king of Israel against Hazael, and was slain by Jehu at the going up to Gur.
Upon his death Athaliah destroyed the seed royal, save Joash, whom Jehosheba hid in the house of the Lord.
scriptures: And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and walked in the way of his father, and in the way of his mother, and in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin:

And Ahaziah fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber that was in Samaria, and was sick: and he sent messengers, and said unto them, Go, enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron whether I shall recover of this disease.
And he walked in the way of the house of Ahab, and did evil in the sight of the LORD, as did the house of Ahab: for he was the son in law of the house of Ahab.

But when Ahaziah the king of Judah saw this, he fled by the way of the garden house. And Jehu followed after him, and said, Smite him also in the chariot. And they did so at the going up to Gur, which is by Ibleam. And he fled to Megiddo, and died there.
corruption_summary: A godly name is treated as though it carried its own power; two Ahaziahs prove that a covenant name on a man who consults Baalzebub is a witness against him, not a shield.
corruption_paragraphs: Both these kings were named for the LORD's grip — 'achaz-Yah, the LORD has taken hold — and both died young and violently in the way of the house of Ahab. The lesson is one Scripture repeats and the modern church constantly forgets: covenant markers are not talismans. Being baptised into a Christian household, carrying a Christian name, holding a church office, and being buried in a churchyard save no one. The men of Jeremiah's day chanted “The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these” (Jer 7:4) and the temple burned. Paul states the principle exactly: “he is not a Jew, which is one outwardly” (Rom 2:28).

The second thing is the sentence in 2Ki 1:2, because it names an alternative worth taking seriously. Ahaziah did not stop believing in supernatural help; he simply sought it from Baalzebub the god of Ekron. Unbelief in Scripture is almost never an empty room. Elijah's question — is it not because there is no God in Israel? — exposes the real offence, which is not doubt but transfer of trust. Every generation has its Ekron: the horoscope, the medium, the manifestation seminar, the “spirituality” that asks nothing of a man and promises to tell him whether he shall recover.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Achazyah (H274), Ahaziah, from 'achaz (H270), to seize, and Yah (H3050); Ba'al Zebub (H1176), lord of the fly.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Achazyah (H274) — Ahaziah; also written 'Achazyahu, whom Jehovah upholds.
Hebrew 'achaz (H270) — to grasp, hold fast; the root of the name and of King Ahaz.
Hebrew Ba'al Zebub (H1176) — Baalzebub, lord of the fly; the Ekronite oracle he consulted.
Greek Beelzeboul (G954) — Beelzebub; by our Lord's day the name of the prince of the devils (Mat 12:24).
Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, enquire of; the verb of consulting an oracle, used of Ahaziah's errand.
usage: “In the way of his father, and in the way of his mother” — a threefold inheritance of sin.
“Go, enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron” — the errand Elijah intercepted.
“He walked in the way of the house of Ahab” — the same verdict in the southern kingdom.

pos: n. (contracted form of Jehoram, borne by contemporary kings of Israel and Judah — the son of Ahab who half-reformed, and the son of Jehoshaphat who murdered his brothers)
etymology: From Hebrew Yoram, a contraction of Yehoram, “the LORD is exalted”, from Yah and rum, to be high. The KJV uses Joram and Jehoram interchangeably, sometimes of the same man in the same chapter.
biblical_def: Joram is the shortened form of Jehoram, and two kings of that name reigned at the same time on either side of the border, married into one another's houses. Joram son of Ahab ruled Israel twelve years, and the Chronicler's verdict on him is unusually qualified: “he wrought evil in the sight of the LORD; but not like his father, and like his mother: for he put away the image of Baal that his father had made” (2Ki 3:2). He kept the calves of Jeroboam, and half-reform is what the phrase “but not like his father” is for. Most of Elisha's public ministry falls in his reign. He was killed by Jehu with an arrow between the shoulders, and his body cast into the plot of Naboth the Jezreelite (2Ki 9:24) — the field where the judgment on Ahab's house had been pronounced. Jehoram of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat, began to reign in his fifth year (2Ki 8:16), married Athaliah the daughter of Ahab, slew all his brethren with the sword, and “walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did the house of Ahab” (2Ki 8:18). He received a writing from Elijah, died of an incurable disease of the bowels, and departed “without being desired”. Two Jorams, one alliance, and a name meaning “the LORD is exalted” over both.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Joram; in sacred history it is a contraction of Jehoram, borne by a king of Israel, the son of Ahab, and a king of Judah, the son of Jehoshaphat.
webster_full: JORAM, n. A contracted form of Jehoram, signifying the Lord is exalted.
Joram the son of Ahab reigned twelve years over Israel, and put away the image of Baal, but cleaved to the sins of Jeroboam.
He warred with Moab and with Syria, and was slain by Jehu in the portion of Naboth the Jezreelite.
Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat reigned eight years over Judah, and slew all his brethren with the sword.
He married the daughter of Ahab, and died of a sore disease, and departed without being desired.
scriptures: And he wrought evil in the sight of the LORD; but not like his father, and like his mother: for he put away the image of Baal that his father had made.
And in the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel, Jehoshaphat being then king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah began to reign.
And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did the house of Ahab: for the daughter of Ahab was his wife: and he did evil in the sight of the LORD.
And Jehu drew a bow with his full strength, and smote Jehoram between his arms, and the arrow went out at his heart, and he sunk down in his chariot.
corruption_summary: Partial reformation is graded as progress; Scripture grades it as evil qualified, and the calves Joram kept destroyed the kingdom the Baal-image he removed had not.
corruption_paragraphs: 2Ki 3:2 is the classic text on half-measures. Joram removed the most conspicuous idol in the land — his father's image of Baal, the very thing Elijah had contended against on Carmel — and the Spirit of God records it, and still says he wrought evil. He kept Jeroboam's calves, which were not a foreign god at all but a convenient way of worshipping the true God: the LORD, at Bethel and Dan, in a form Israel had chosen. That is the sin the northern kingdom died of, and it is far more durable than open paganism because it wears the right name. The regulative principle of worship is the church's protection here: what God has not commanded in His worship is not permitted, however sincerely it is offered to Him.

The second corruption is the alliance itself. Jehoshaphat was a good king who made one persistent mistake — he married his son to Ahab's daughter for the sake of national unity. The fruit of it was Jehoram murdering his brothers, Athaliah nearly extinguishing the line of David, and two generations of Baal worship in Jerusalem. The seer Jehu had asked Jehoshaphat the question directly: “Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD?” (2Ch 19:2). Good men make dynastic bargains with evil houses for reasons that look like prudence, and their grandchildren pay.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yoram (H3141) and Yehoram (H3088), from Yah (H3050) and rum (H7311), to be exalted.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yehoram (H3088) — Jehoram, “the LORD is exalted”; the full form of the name.
Hebrew Yoram (H3141) — Joram; the contraction, used of the same men interchangeably.
Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, to be lifted up; the root of the theophoric element.
Hebrew matstsebah (H4676) — a standing image or pillar; the Baal-image Joram removed (2Ki 3:2).
Hebrew chelqah (H2513) — a portion of ground; Naboth's plot, where Joram's body was cast (2Ki 9:25-26).
usage: “But not like his father, and like his mother” — reform measured and found short.
“The daughter of Ahab was his wife” — the marriage that poisoned Judah.
“Smote Jehoram between his arms” — judgment overtaking a house in Naboth's field.

pos: n. (the father of Jeroboam — a man of whom nothing is recorded but his son, and whose name became the standing epitaph of the northern kingdom)
etymology: From Hebrew Nebat, from nabat, to look, to regard, to behold. He is an Ephrathite of Zereda, husband of Zeruah, and Scripture tells us nothing further about him.
biblical_def: Nebat is one of the strangest names in the Bible, because he does nothing and is mentioned more than twenty times. He appears once as a fact of ancestry — “Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephrathite of Zereda, Solomon's servant, whose mother's name was Zeruah, a widow woman” (1Ki 11:26) — and thereafter only as half of a formula. The books of Kings assess every northern king by one measure, and the measure is Nebat's son: he walked “in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin”. Nadab did, and Baasha, and Zimri, and Omri, and Ahab, and Ahaziah, and Joram, and Jehu, and every king down to Hoshea, in whose ninth year Samaria fell. The historian will not let the phrase go, because the calves at Bethel and Dan set up for political convenience — so the people would not go up to Jerusalem to sacrifice — were the founding act of the kingdom and its cause of death. 2Ki 17:21 states the whole doctrine of the northern kingdom in one verse: Jeroboam “drave Israel from following the LORD, and made them sin a great sin.” Nebat's only recorded achievement is to have fathered him, and his name is chiselled onto the tombstone of ten tribes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Nebat; in sacred history he is the father of Jeroboam the first king of Israel after the division, an Ephrathite of Zereda.
webster_full: NEBAT, n. An Ephrathite of Zereda, father of Jeroboam the first king of the ten tribes.
The name is derived from a verb signifying to look or behold.
Nothing is recorded of him but his parentage of Jeroboam and the name of his wife Zeruah.
The phrase Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin, is the constant formula of the book of Kings.
It is repeated of every king of Israel from Nadab to Hoshea.
scriptures: And Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephrathite of Zereda, Solomon's servant, whose mother's name was Zeruah, a widow woman, even he lifted up his hand against the king.
And he shall give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, who did sin, and who made Israel to sin.
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin.
For he rent Israel from the house of David; and they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat king: and Jeroboam drave Israel from following the LORD, and made them sin a great sin.
corruption_summary: Scripture's insistence on repeating one formula for two hundred years reads as tedium; it is in fact a doctrine — that a founder's sin becomes a nation's inheritance, and every successor either repents of it or ratifies it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the formula exists to teach. Modern readers skim past “the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, wherewith he made Israel to sin” as a copyist's refrain. It is nothing of the kind; it is the historian's doctrine of institutional sin. Jeroboam did not merely sin; he built his sin into the constitution of a kingdom — two calves, a rival priesthood not of Levi, and a feast in the eighth month “which he had devised of his own heart” (1Ki 12:33). Nineteen kings followed and not one of them dismantled it. A church, a denomination, or a family can be set on a footing that every later generation must either tear up or perpetuate, and passivity is perpetuation.

Nebat himself is the second lesson, a quieter one. He is a name in a genealogy, dead before the story starts, and his name is spoken more often in Scripture than most of the kings who followed — always attached to a catastrophe he did not commit. Fathers cast longer shadows than they think, and a man may be remembered chiefly by what his son does with what he was given. The counterweight in Scripture is exact: “the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Eze 18:20) — each man answers for himself. But influence and guilt are different things, and a father should be sober about the first even while he is not accountable for the second.
roots_summary: Hebrew Nebat (H5028), from nabat (H5027), to look, behold, regard.
roots_lines: Hebrew Nebat (H5028) — Nebat; found only as the patronymic of Jeroboam.
Hebrew nabat (H5027) — to look, to regard; the root, used of God looking upon the afflicted.
Hebrew chata' (H2398) — to sin, to miss; in the causative stem, “made Israel to sin”.
Hebrew 'egel (H5695) — a calf; the two golden calves of Bethel and Dan (1Ki 12:28).
Hebrew nadach (H5080) — to drive away, thrust out; “drave Israel from following the LORD” (2Ki 17:21).
usage: “Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephrathite of Zereda” — the one thing recorded of him.
“Who made Israel to sin” — the formula repeated over nineteen reigns.
“Drave Israel from following the LORD” — the epitaph of the northern kingdom.

pos: n. (high priest under Josiah — the man who found the book of the law in the house of the LORD, and set a reformation going)
etymology: From Hebrew Chilqiyah, “my portion is the LORD”, from cheleq, a portion or inheritance, and Yah. Several men bear the name, including the father of Jeremiah and the father of Eliakim the steward.
biblical_def: Hilkiah was high priest in the eighteenth year of Josiah, and one sentence of his changed the history of Judah: “I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD” (2Ki 22:8). The circumstances are worth weighing. Money was being counted for temple repairs; the priest was going through the house; and there, in the building whose entire reason for existing was the covenant, the covenant document had been mislaid. Chronicles specifies what it was: “a book of the law of the LORD given by Moses” (2Ch 34:14). Hilkiah gave it to Shaphan the scribe, Shaphan read it to the king, and the king rent his clothes, because he heard in it the curses of Deuteronomy pronounced on exactly the nation he was governing. From that hearing came the deputation to Huldah the prophetess, the covenant renewed at the temple door, and the fiercest purge in Judah's history — “the king commanded Hilkiah the high priest… to bring forth out of the temple of the LORD all the vessels that were made for Baal, and for the grove, and for all the host of heaven” (2Ki 23:4). Hilkiah found the book and then carried out what it said. He is the pattern of a faithful minister: he did not compose the word, he did not soften it, he handed it over and obeyed it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Hilkiah; in sacred history he is the high priest in the reign of Josiah who found the book of the law in the house of the Lord.
webster_full: HILKIAH, n. The high priest in the days of Josiah, king of Judah; the name signifies my portion is Jehovah.
While the money for the repair of the temple was told out, he found the book of the law.
He delivered it to Shaphan the scribe, who read it before the king.
By the king's command he went with others to enquire of Huldah the prophetess.
He executed the purging of the temple of the vessels of Baal and of the host of heaven.
scriptures: And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.
And when they brought out the money that was brought into the house of the LORD, Hilkiah the priest found a book of the law of the LORD given by Moses.

And the king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, and the priests of the second order, and the keepers of the door, to bring forth out of the temple of the LORD all the vessels that were made for Baal, and for the grove, and for all the host of heaven: and he burned them without Jerusalem in the fields of Kidron, and carried the ashes of them unto Bethel.
And when they had called to the king, there came out to them Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, which was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah the son of Asaph the recorder.
corruption_summary: Critical scholarship treats Hilkiah's find as a pious forgery composed to justify Josiah's policy; the theory requires the high priest, the scribe, the king, and the prophetess to be in on a fraud that condemned them.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard critical reconstruction, running from de Wette in 1805 through the documentary school, holds that the book Hilkiah produced was Deuteronomy, newly written to authorise the centralisation of worship at Jerusalem, and planted to be found. The dictionary rejects it, and the reasons are not merely confessional. A document manufactured to support a policy does not open by condemning the men who commissioned it and promising national destruction; Josiah's reaction was to rend his clothes and be told that the evil would come, only not in his days. Nor does a forger send to a prophetess for independent authentication. Chronicles calls it what it is — the law of the LORD given by Moses — and the dictionary holds Mosaic authorship of the Torah. The find is a rediscovery, which is exactly what one expects after fifty-five years of Manasseh.

The living corruption is the plainer one: a Bible lost inside a church. Judah had priests, sacrifices, a functioning temple, an active building programme, and no copy of the covenant in use. The forms outlived the word. It is possible for a congregation to keep every ordinance, meet every week, and manage its property well, while nobody present could say what the book requires — and the first sign of real reformation is always the same, a man reading the text aloud and a hearer tearing his clothes. Nehemiah 8 is the same scene, and so was Wittenberg.
roots_summary: Hebrew Chilqiyah (H2518), Hilkiah, from cheleq (H2506), a portion, and Yah (H3050); sepher hat-torah (H5612 + H8451), the book of the law.
roots_lines: Hebrew Chilqiyah (H2518) — Hilkiah, “my portion is the LORD”; the priestly name of Josiah's day.
Hebrew cheleq (H2506) — a portion, share; the Levites' inheritance was the LORD Himself (Num 18:20).
Hebrew sepher (H5612) — a book, scroll, writing; the thing found in the house.
Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction, direction; from yarah, to cast or point out the way.
Hebrew matsa' (H4672) — to find, to come upon; the verb of 2Ki 22:8, discovery rather than composition.
usage: “I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD” — the sentence that began a reformation.
“A book of the law of the LORD given by Moses” — the Chronicler's identification of it.
“The king commanded Hilkiah the high priest” — the finder made the purger.

pos: n. (Hezekiah's steward, the man given the key of the house of David; also the birth-name of king Jehoiakim)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Elyaqim, “God raises up”, from 'El, God, and qum, to rise or establish. The name is fulfilled precisely in Isa 22, where God says He will call His servant Eliakim and clothe him.
biblical_def: Two men named Eliakim matter, and they stand at opposite ends of the same century. The first is Hezekiah's steward, “which was over the household” (2Ki 18:18), who stood on the wall to answer Rabshakeh and afterward went in sackcloth to Isaiah. Isa 22 makes him a type. Shebna the self-important treasurer, hewing himself a sepulchre on high, is to be pulled down, and God says: “I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah” (Isa 22:20), robe him, gird him, commit the government into his hand, and — the great verse — “the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open” (Isa 22:22). The risen Christ takes those exact words to Himself in the letter to Philadelphia (Rev 3:7). Eliakim is a nail fastened in a sure place, a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, a steward of a house not his own. The second Eliakim is the son of Josiah, whom Pharaohnechoh made king “and turned his name to Jehoiakim” (2Ki 23:34) — a puppet renamed by the man who installed him, and the king who cut Jeremiah's scroll with a penknife and burned it. One Eliakim carried the key; the other burned the word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Eliakim; in sacred history it names the steward of Hezekiah's household and the son of Josiah whose name Pharaoh changed to Jehoiakim.
webster_full: ELIAKIM, n. The son of Hilkiah, steward or governor of the household of Hezekiah king of Judah.
The name signifies God shall raise up, or whom God establishes.
He was sent with Shebna and Joah to treat with Rabshakeh, and afterward to Isaiah the prophet.
Isaiah foretold that the key of the house of David should be laid upon his shoulder.
Also, the son of Josiah, whom Pharaohnechoh made king and named Jehoiakim.
scriptures: And when they had called to the king, there came out to them Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, which was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah the son of Asaph the recorder.
And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah:
And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open.
And Pharaohnechoh made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in the room of Josiah his father, and turned his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away: and he came to Egypt, and died there.
corruption_summary: Isa 22:22 has been claimed by Rome as the charter of the papal keys; the risen Christ applies the verse to Himself, and He does not delegate the key He holds.
corruption_paragraphs: Roman apologetics reads Isa 22:22 as the Old Testament pattern behind Mat 16:19, and infers a perpetual office of prime minister of the kingdom, held by Peter and transmitted to his successors at Rome. The New Testament settles the identification itself, and not in Rome's favour: “These things saith he that is holy, he that is true, he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth” (Rev 3:7). The verse is applied to the Lord Jesus, in His own words, without qualification. What He gives the church in Mat 16 and 18 is the ministerial use of the keys — preaching and discipline, binding and loosing by declaring His word — which the Reformers understood and which belongs to the eldership of a local congregation, not to a single bishop over the whole. The 1689 Confession holds two offices in the church, elder and deacon, and no third above them.

The second thing is Shebna, who is the whole reason Eliakim is promoted. Shebna was over the house and was spending his office on his own monument. God's judgment on him is one of the most physical in the prophets: He will surely violently turn and toss him like a ball into a large country, “and there the chariots of thy glory shall be the shame of thy lord's house” (Isa 22:18). A steward exists for his master's house. When a man in office begins building his own name inside it, God has been known to replace him publicly, and to name his successor in advance.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Elyaqim (H471), from 'El (H410), God, and qum (H6965), to arise; maphteach (H4668), a key.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Elyaqim (H471) — Eliakim, “God raises up”; fulfilled literally in Isa 22:20.
Hebrew qum (H6965) — to rise, stand, establish; the root of the promise in the name.
Hebrew maphteach (H4668) — a key, an opener; laid upon the shoulder as a badge of office.
Hebrew 'al hab-bayith — “over the household”; the office of chief steward of the palace.
Greek kleis (G2807) — a key; used by the risen Christ of the key of David (Rev 3:7).
usage: “I will call my servant Eliakim” — a name that was also a prophecy.
“The key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder” — the office Christ claims.
“Turned his name to Jehoiakim” — a king renamed by the power that owned him.

pos: n. (a common Hebrew name borne both by the false prophet who broke Jeremiah's yoke and by the captive who would not bow at Dura)
etymology: From Hebrew Chananyah, “the LORD hath been gracious”, from chanan, to show favour, and Yah. Some fifteen men bear it in Scripture; the Greek form is Ananias.
biblical_def: Hananiah is a common and beautiful name — the LORD has been gracious — and Scripture attaches it to two men who define opposite ends of faithfulness. The first is Hananiah of Gibeon, a prophet, who stood in the house of the LORD before the priests and all the people and contradicted Jeremiah with a comforting oracle: within two years Babylon's yoke would be broken and the vessels returned. Then “Hananiah the prophet took the yoke from off the prophet Jeremiah's neck, and brake it” (Jer 28:10), and repeated his promise. Jeremiah went his way, came back with a word, and delivered the sentence: “Hear now, Hananiah; The LORD hath not sent thee; but thou makest this people to trust in a lie” (Jer 28:15). He was told he would die that year, and “so Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month” (Jer 28:17). The second Hananiah is one of the four Judean youths taken to Babylon — “Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah” (Dan 1:6) — renamed Shadrach by the prince of the eunuchs, and known ever after by the name a pagan gave him. He stood before the furnace and said that God was able to deliver, and if not, they still would not serve the golden image. One Hananiah promised deliverance God had not promised; the other refused to demand a deliverance God had not promised.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Hananiah; in sacred history it is a frequent Hebrew name, borne notably by a false prophet of Gibeon and by the companion of Daniel called Shadrach.
webster_full: HANANIAH, n. A Hebrew name signifying the grace or mercy of Jehovah; in Greek, Ananias.
Hananiah the son of Azur, a prophet of Gibeon, withstood Jeremiah and brake the yoke from his neck.
Being told by Jeremiah that he should die that year, he died in the seventh month.
Hananiah, one of the children of Judah carried to Babylon, was named Shadrach by the prince of the eunuchs.
The name is borne also by a captain of the ward in Nehemiah, and by several Levites and princes.
scriptures: Then Hananiah the prophet took the yoke from off the prophet Jeremiah's neck, and brake it.
Then said the prophet Jeremiah unto Hananiah the prophet, Hear now, Hananiah; The LORD hath not sent thee; but thou makest this people to trust in a lie.
So Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month.
Dan 1:6
Now among these were of the children of Judah, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah:
corruption_summary: The mark of the false prophet is taken to be doctrinal strangeness; Hananiah's message was orthodox, patriotic, encouraging, and delivered in the temple — and it was a lie.
corruption_paragraphs: Everything about Hananiah looked right. He said “Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel”; he prophesied in the house of the LORD; he promised the restoration of the vessels and the return of the captives; and he performed a prophetic sign, breaking a yoke, exactly as the true prophets did. He was also more encouraging than Jeremiah, which is generally what a congregation is buying. Jeremiah's own reply is startlingly generous — “Amen: the LORD do so” — before he says the thing that decides it: the prophets before us prophesied war and evil, so the prophet who prophesies peace will be known when his word comes to pass. The test Scripture gives is not warmth and not orthodoxy of vocabulary; it is whether the LORD sent him, evidenced by whether the thing happens (Deu 18:22). The modern equivalents are the prosperity announcement, the date-set for the Lord's return, and the “word” delivered over a congregation that no one afterwards audits.

The name itself is the second sermon. Both men were called “the LORD has been gracious.” One traded on the grace of God as a guarantee of comfortable outcomes; the other confessed it while telling a king that God might not deliver him and that he would not bow either way. Grace received rightly makes a man able to stand in front of a furnace; grace presumed upon makes him break other men's yokes and tell them what they wish to hear.
roots_summary: Hebrew Chananyah (H2608), from chanan (H2603), to be gracious, and Yah (H3050); Greek Hananias (G367).
roots_lines: Hebrew Chananyah (H2608) — Hananiah, “the LORD hath been gracious”.
Hebrew chanan (H2603) — to bend or stoop in kindness, to show favour; the root of chen, grace.
Hebrew motah (H4133) — a yoke-bar; the thing Jeremiah wore and Hananiah broke (Jer 28:10).
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — a lie, falsehood; what Hananiah made the people trust in.
Aramaic Shadrak (H7715) — Shadrach; the Babylonian name given to Hananiah in Dan 1:7.
usage: “Took the yoke… and brake it” — a false sign performed in the temple.
“Thou makest this people to trust in a lie” — the charge that decided the contest.
“Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah” — four captives who kept their God and lost their names.

pos: n. (the priest and temple governor who beat Jeremiah and put him in the stocks — renamed by the prophet Magor-missabib, Terror on every side)
etymology: From Hebrew Pashchur, of uncertain meaning; a splitting or a freedom has been proposed, and an Egyptian derivation “portion of Horus” is possible. Whatever it meant, Jeremiah replaced it with one that could not be mistaken.
biblical_def: Pashur the son of Immer was a priest and “chief governor in the house of the LORD” (Jer 20:1) — the temple's chief officer of order, responsible for keeping the peace in its courts. He kept it in the usual way: “Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD” (Jer 20:2). A prophet flogged and pilloried overnight, by the man whose office was the sanctity of the sanctuary, at its own gate. In the morning Pashur let him out, and Jeremiah gave him a new name: “The LORD hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magormissabib” (Jer 20:3) — Terror round about — and a sentence: “thou shalt come to Babylon, and there thou shalt die, and shalt be buried there, thou, and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied lies” (Jer 20:6). It is out of that night in the stocks that the darkest of the prophet's confessions comes, the passage that begins “O LORD, thou hast deceived me” and ends with the fire shut up in his bones. A different Pashur, son of Melchiah, later carries Zedekiah's enquiry to Jeremiah and joins those who cast him into the miry dungeon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Pashur; in sacred history he is the priest and governor of the temple who smote Jeremiah and set him in the stocks.
webster_full: PASHUR, n. The son of Immer, a priest and chief governor in the house of the Lord in the days of Jehoiakim.
He smote Jeremiah and put him in the stocks in the high gate of Benjamin.
Jeremiah on the morrow called his name Magormissabib, that is, terror round about.
He was foretold that he should go captive to Babylon and die there with all his friends.
Another Pashur, the son of Melchiah, was sent by Zedekiah to enquire of the Lord by Jeremiah.
scriptures: Jer 20:1
Now Pashur the son of Immer the priest, who was also chief governor in the house of the LORD, heard that Jeremiah prophesied these things.
Jer 20:2
Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD.
Jer 20:3
And it came to pass on the morrow, that Pashur brought forth Jeremiah out of the stocks. Then said Jeremiah unto him, The LORD hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magormissabib.
Jer 20:6

And thou, Pashur, and all that dwell in thine house shall go into captivity: and thou shalt come to Babylon, and there thou shalt die, and shalt be buried there, thou, and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied lies.
corruption_summary: Persecution is imagined as coming from outside the church; Jeremiah's stocks stood at the temple gate and were ordered by the temple's own officer.
corruption_paragraphs: Pashur is the reminder that the sharpest opposition to the word of God has usually come from inside the religious establishment. He was not a Babylonian; he was a priest, of the course of Immer, holding a real office in the real temple of the true God, and he had the whip out because a preacher had said the city would fall. The pattern runs through Scripture — the prophets stoned in the courts, the Lord Jesus delivered up by the chief priests, Stephen killed by the council, Paul's worst dangers “in perils among false brethren” (2Co 11:26). A church can build a whole apparatus of order whose practical function is to keep unwelcome truth out of its own courts, and the men who run it will believe they are defending holiness.

The second thing is the renaming, because it shows how God answers this. Jeremiah does not fight back and does not appeal; he pronounces a name. Magor-missabib, terror on every side, is a phrase Jeremiah uses of the coming invasion, and now it is fastened to the man who thought himself the guardian of safety. The one who put the prophet in stocks to stop the word about Babylon will himself die in Babylon. And Jer 20:7-9, written the same morning, keeps the account honest about the cost: the prophet accuses God of overpowering him, resolves to speak no more in His name, and finds the word “as a burning fire shut up in my bones” that he could not stay. Faithfulness in that chapter is not serenity; it is being unable to stop.
roots_summary: Hebrew Pashchur (H6583), Pashur; Magor mis-Sabib (H4036), terror round about; mahpeketh (H4115), the stocks.
roots_lines: Hebrew Pashchur (H6583) — Pashur; borne by several priests, two of them opponents of Jeremiah.
Hebrew Magor mis-Sabib (H4036) — Magormissabib, “terror on every side”; Jeremiah's renaming of him.
Hebrew mahpeketh (H4115) — the stocks; from haphak, to overturn, because the body was twisted in them.
Hebrew paqid nagid — chief governor, overseer; the temple police office Pashur held (Jer 20:1).
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — a lie; “to whom thou hast prophesied lies” (Jer 20:6).
usage: “Chief governor in the house of the LORD” — the office that ordered the beating.
“Put him in the stocks… by the house of the LORD” — persecution at the sanctuary gate.
“Not… Pashur, but Magormissabib” — a name the prophet gave and God kept.

pos: n. (the scribe in whose chamber the roll of Jeremiah was laid up before Jehoiakim burned it; also a prince of Ephraim and a son of David)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Elishama', “God hath heard”, from 'El, God, and shama', to hear. Several men bear it: the prince of Ephraim in the wilderness census, a son of David born in Jerusalem, a teaching priest under Jehoshaphat, and the scribe of Jeremiah's day.
biblical_def: Elishama the scribe holds a small and terrible place in the thirty-sixth chapter of Jeremiah. Baruch had written the prophet's words on a roll and read them in the temple; Michaiah reported it, and the princes sent for Baruch. The scene is set in Elishama's room: “he went down into the king's house, into the scribe's chamber: and, lo, all the princes sat there, even Elishama the scribe” (Jer 36:12). They heard it read, were afraid, told Baruch to hide himself and Jeremiah with him, and then made a decision that has an official smell to it — “they laid up the roll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe” (Jer 36:20) and went to the king with a verbal summary. Jehoiakim sent Jehudi to fetch it: “he took it out of Elishama the scribe's chamber” (Jer 36:21), and read three or four leaves at a time, and the king cut them with a penknife and burned them, and none of them were afraid, nor rent their garments. The word of God was filed in a civil servant's office and then destroyed page by page in a winter brazier. God's answer is the point of the chapter: Jeremiah took another roll, Baruch wrote it again, “and there were added besides unto them many like words”.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Elishama; in sacred history it names a prince of Ephraim in the wilderness, a son of David, and the scribe in whose chamber Jeremiah's roll was laid.
webster_full: ELISHAMA, n. A Hebrew name signifying God hath heard.
Elishama the son of Ammihud was prince of the children of Ephraim in the wilderness, and grandfather of Joshua.
A son of David born unto him in Jerusalem bore the same name.
Elishama, a priest, was sent by Jehoshaphat to teach the law in the cities of Judah.
Elishama the scribe had a chamber in the king's house, where the roll of Jeremiah was laid up before Jehoiakim burned it.
scriptures: Then he went down into the king's house, into the scribe's chamber: and, lo, all the princes sat there, even Elishama the scribe, and Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, and Elnathan the son of Achbor, and Gemariah the son of Shaphan, and Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes.
And they went in to the king into the court, but they laid up the roll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe, and told all the words in the ears of the king.

So the king sent Jehudi to fetch the roll: and he took it out of Elishama the scribe's chamber. And Jehudi read it in the ears of the king, and in the ears of all the princes which stood beside the king.

And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.
corruption_summary: The burning of a scroll is taken as proof that the Bible is a fragile human artifact; the chapter records the burning precisely in order to report that the words were written again, and more added.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 36 is the Bible's own account of an attempt to destroy the Bible, and it is remarkably unbothered. The king had the physical roll and burned it completely; the LORD said take another roll and write in it all the former words, “and there were added besides unto them many like words” (Jer 36:32). The doctrine of preservation the dictionary holds is not a claim that no manuscript was ever lost or burned — many were — but that God has providentially preserved His word through every such attempt, so that what He said remains available to His church. Diocletian burned copies, and there are more today. The 1689 Confession states it: the Scriptures were “by his singular care and providence kept pure in all ages.”

The corruption to name in Elishama himself is quieter and closer to home. He and the princes were afraid when they heard the roll — genuinely alarmed, alarmed enough to warn Baruch to hide. And then they filed it. They summarised the contents for the king rather than putting the text in his hands, they let the roll sit in an office, and when Jehudi came for it they did not stand in the doorway. Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah at least made intercession that the king should not burn it. Being moved by the word and taking no risk for it is the characteristic sin of the respectable, and it is how a document that alarms everybody ends up in a drawer.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Elishama' (H476), from 'El (H410), God, and shama' (H8085), to hear; sopher (H5608), a scribe; megillah (H4039), a roll.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Elishama' (H476) — Elishama, “God hath heard”.
Hebrew shama' (H8085) — to hear, and so to obey; the root that indicts the men of Jer 36 who heard and did not.
Hebrew sopher (H5608) — a scribe, a writer, one who counts; the civil-service office of the king's house.
Hebrew megillah (H4039) — a roll, scroll; the form of the book Baruch wrote and Jehoiakim burned.
Hebrew ta'ar has-sopher — the scribe's penknife; the tool for trimming reeds, turned into an instrument against the word.
usage: “All the princes sat there, even Elishama the scribe” — the room where the roll was heard.
“They laid up the roll in the chamber of Elishama” — the word filed rather than obeyed.
“He cut it with the penknife” — a king's answer to what he had heard.

pos: n. (a very common Hebrew name in the last century of Judah — borne by the governor of Josiah's city, by priests, Levites, and by fathers of both a true and a false prophet)
etymology: From Hebrew Ma'aseyah, “the work of the LORD”, from ma'aseh, a work or deed, and Yah. Roughly twenty men bear the name, nearly all of them in the reigns from Josiah to the return.
biblical_def: Maaseiah is one of those names that shows how densely populated the last chapters of the kingdom were with ordinary faithful men. The best-known is “Maaseiah the governor of the city” (2Ch 34:8), one of the three officials Josiah sent to repair the house of the LORD — the civil magistrate of Jerusalem employed in a work of reformation, which is what a Christian magistrate is for. Others carry the name into the crisis: Zephaniah the priest, who twice carried Zedekiah's enquiries to Jeremiah, is “the son of Maaseiah” (Jer 21:1); another Maaseiah is “the keeper of the door” whose chamber stood in the temple (Jer 35:4), where Jeremiah tested the Rechabites with wine they would not drink. But one of them fathered a man who ruined the name: Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, one of the two false prophets in Babylon whom Jeremiah says the king of Babylon roasted in the fire (Jer 29:21-22). After the exile the name reappears among the priests who put away strange wives, among those who stood by Ezra at the reading of the law, and among the singers at the dedication of the wall. The name means “the work of the LORD”, and its bearers are almost all in the second rank — doorkeepers, governors, singers, fathers — which is where most of that work is done.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Maaseiah; in sacred history it is a frequent Hebrew name signifying the work of Jehovah, borne by priests, Levites, princes and doorkeepers.
webster_full: MAASEIAH, n. A Hebrew name signifying the work of Jehovah.
Maaseiah was governor of the city of Jerusalem under Josiah, and was employed in repairing the temple.
Maaseiah the son of Shallum was keeper of the door, and had a chamber in the house of the Lord.
Zephaniah the priest, sent by Zedekiah to Jeremiah, was the son of a Maaseiah.
The name is borne by several who returned from the captivity, and who stood with Ezra at the reading of the law.
scriptures: Now in the eighteenth year of his reign, when he had purged the land, and the house, he sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, and Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah the son of Joahaz the recorder, to repair the house of the LORD his God.
Jer 21:1
The word which came unto Jeremiah from the LORD, when king Zedekiah sent unto him Pashur the son of Melchiah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, saying,
Jer 35:4

And I brought them into the house of the LORD, into the chamber of the sons of Hanan, the son of Igdaliah, a man of God, which was by the chamber of the princes, which was above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, the keeper of the door:

Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, of Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and of Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, which prophesy a lie unto you in my name; Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall slay them before your eyes;
corruption_summary: Long lists of unfamiliar Hebrew names are skipped as filler; they are the record of the ordinary men by whom reformation was actually carried out, and Scripture troubles to keep them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of the second rank. A reader who skips the Maaseiahs is skipping the men who did the work: the governor who organised the temple repairs, the doorkeeper who had a room where a prophet could examine the Rechabites, the priest's father, the singer at the wall. Scripture's habit of preserving these names is a doctrine in itself — the Lord keeps a book of remembrance for “them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name” (Mal 3:16). Reformations are announced by a Josiah and are executed by a hundred Maaseiahs.

The other thing this name teaches is the limit of heritage. One Maaseiah fathered Zephaniah the priest, who carried a king's enquiry to a prophet and afterwards received Shemaiah's letter demanding Jeremiah be put in the stocks — and who read that letter aloud to Jeremiah instead. Another Maaseiah fathered Zedekiah, whom God names as prophesying a lie and who died in Babylon in the fire. Same name, same generation, same nation, opposite ends. A godly household is a means of grace and is not a guarantee, and the reason is the one Ezekiel gives: every soul answers for itself.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ma'aseyah (H4641), from ma'aseh (H4639), a work or deed, and Yah (H3050); shomer has-saph, keeper of the door.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ma'aseyah (H4641) — Maaseiah, “the work of the LORD”; also written Ma'aseyahu.
Hebrew ma'aseh (H4639) — a work, deed, business; from 'asah, to do or make.
Hebrew saph (H5592) — a threshold, doorway; the keepers of the door were a real temple office (2Ki 25:18).
Hebrew sar ha-'ir — governor of the city; the office Maaseiah held under Josiah.
Hebrew lishkah (H3957) — a chamber, cell; the temple rooms where business and testing were done.
usage: “Maaseiah the governor of the city” — the magistrate at work on the house of God.
“Maaseiah the son of Shallum, the keeper of the door” — an office with a room in it.
“Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, which prophesy a lie” — the same name at the other end.

pos: n. (the father of Isaiah the prophet — named in the superscription of the greatest of the prophetic books and nowhere else described)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Amots, strong, from 'amats, to be strong or courageous. He is not to be confused with the prophet Amos, whose name is a different Hebrew word, 'Amos, a burden-bearer.
biblical_def: Amoz is known by one relationship. Thirteen times Scripture calls the prophet “Isaiah the son of Amoz”, and nothing else is recorded of the man — not his tribe, not his trade, not a word he spoke. He opens the book: “The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah” (Isa 1:1), and heads the major sections after it (Isa 2:1; Isa 13:1). When Hezekiah sends his officers in sackcloth in the worst hour of the Assyrian siege, they are sent “to Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz” (2Ki 19:2), the patronymic still attached at the crisis of the kingdom. Jewish tradition, which the dictionary reports without endorsing, makes Amoz a brother of king Amaziah and so places Isaiah in the royal family, which would explain the prophet's access to kings and his command of court and diplomatic language. Scripture does not say so. What Scripture does is fix a name in the superscription of sixty-six chapters, so that the book announces itself as the vision of a particular man, son of a particular father, in the reigns of four named kings — a prophecy with an address, not an anonymous oracle.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Amoz; in sacred history he is the father of the prophet Isaiah, distinguished from Amos the herdman of Tekoa.
webster_full: AMOZ, n. The father of Isaiah the prophet; the name signifies strong.
He is named only in the title of the prophecy and in the books of Kings and Chronicles.
He is not the same with Amos, the herdman of Tekoa, whose name is written differently in the Hebrew.
The Jewish writers make him the brother of Amaziah, king of Judah, but this rests on tradition only.
The repeated designation Isaiah the son of Amoz distinguishes the prophet in the sacred records.
scriptures: Isa 1:1
The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.
Isa 2:1
The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem.
Isa 13:1
The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see.
And he sent Eliakim, which was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz.
corruption_summary: The recurring superscription “Isaiah the son of Amoz” is the book's own claim to a single eighth-century author; the division of Isaiah into two or three prophets is asserted against it.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical division of Isaiah into a first prophet of the eighth century and one or two later writers is the standard position of the academy, and the reason offered is that chapters 40 and following address the exile as a present reality and name Cyrus, who was not born. That reasoning excludes predictive prophecy before examining the text, which is a philosophical commitment rather than a finding. The book itself names one author in three superscriptions, always as the son of Amoz. The New Testament quotes from both halves and attributes both to the same man — in one passage John cites chapter 53 and chapter 6 in consecutive verses and says “Esaias said again” (Joh 12:39-41). The Lord Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth was handed “the book of the prophet Esaias” (Luk 4:17) and read chapter 61 from it. The dictionary holds one Isaiah, and holds it on the authority of the Lord who read him.

The second thing to say about Amoz is pastoral. He is a name and a fatherhood, with no recorded words. Most Christian men will be that: not the prophet, but the father of one; not the reformer, but the household in which a reformer was catechised. Scripture's way of honouring such men is not to write their biographies but to keep their names permanently attached to what their children did. Thirteen times, across three books and seven centuries of transmission, someone had to write “the son of Amoz.”
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Amots (H531), Amoz, from 'amats (H553), to be strong, alert, courageous; distinct from 'Amos (H5986).
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Amots (H531) — Amoz, “strong”; the father of Isaiah.
Hebrew 'amats (H553) — to be strong, to confirm; the word of Jos 1:9, “be strong and of a good courage”.
Hebrew 'Amos (H5986) — Amos, a burden-bearer; a different name and a different man, the herdman of Tekoa.
Hebrew Yesha'yahu (H3470) — Isaiah, “the salvation of the LORD”; the theme of the whole book in the prophet's name.
Hebrew chazon (H2377) — a vision; the word that opens the book (Isa 1:1).
usage: “The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz” — a prophecy with an author and an address.
“The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see” — the same name over the later oracles.
“To Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz” — the patronymic still attached in the siege.
